title: Asa di Var close
hookLine: wonder, awe, sweetness, the thread of compassion

lines: ONE LINE CARRIED OUT THE DOOR.
cards: When the dawn singing ends, the sangat doesn't scatter right away. People stand for Ardas. Karah prashad, the warm sweet offering, is passed hand to hand.
Someone folds the white sheets. Outside, the sun is up and the streets are filling with buses and school uniforms. People walk out carrying almost nothing: no notes, no book.
Maybe one line, still humming in the back of the head. That's one way the var travels: as lines people carry out the door.

teach.h: THE BALLAD, THE GURU, THE MOONS.
teach.b: Let's walk the staircase once, from the top. An old ballad of heroes, given new words and sung to a king's tune. A sacrifice to the Guru a hundred times a day, the Guru who made angels out of men.
A hundred moons, and still dark without the Guru. The One who made Himself and watches with delight.

Then four steps of seeing: vismaad, wonder at every sound and color; kudrat, power in seeing, eating, loving; bhau, the wind and rivers moving in awe; and nirbhau, nirankar, only the Formless without fear.
Then the people: the contented ones who served. Haumai, ego as a chronic illness with its medicine inside it. Cartloads of books, and only one thing counted.
Koorh, the false king and everything that passes. Sach, truth known only when the heart is true. Then the turnings: pain the medicine, pleasure the disease.
Mitthat neevee, sweetness and humility, the heavy side of the scale. The silk-cotton tree, tall and useless. The sacrifice to the Guru who put wisdom on the eyes.

teach.h: THE THREAD, THE SERVANT, THE DAWN.
teach.b: Then the thread: compassion the cotton, contentment the thread, restraint the knot, truth the twist; a thread that won't break, burn, stain or be lost. Sootak moved inside: greed, lies, coveting, gossip.
Fikka words that make a fikka life. The servant who argues. And the shape itself: pauris as steps, Guru Angad's second voice, the whole thing sung as the sky turns gold.
If one thread runs through it all, it might be the one in the carry.
The var keeps starting with wonder. Before it corrects anyone, it makes them look. Wonder first, then the work.

how: Sikhs hear the Asa di Var sung in gurdwaras each morning, followed by Ardas and karah prashad, and many carry a favorite salok from it through the day.

o: a hymn sung only at the close of the day
wonder, the awe that comes from looking
fear of the One's judgment and power

games.q: the dawn ballad — tap the pairs.

s: the Asa di Var begins by correcting people
it keeps starting with wonder: before it corrects anyone, it makes them look.
the pauris are Guru Nanak's and some saloks are Guru Angad's
the Asa di Var is sung aloud at dawn, not only read
sung at dawn, carried out the door.

games.q: the dawn singing has ended and you're walking out into the morning. what do you carry?
o: one line that keeps coming back.
nothing; it stays in the gurdwara.
games.why: that's how the var travels: one line, still humming in the back of the head, carried out the door.

practice: Let the block pass through your mind once more, bhau, the simmal, the scale, the thread, dal without salt, the arguing servant, and wait for the one that keeps coming back.
Say its picture to yourself in one sentence, then breathe with it, the way the sangat carries a line out the door. If you pray, you can say Waheguru.

wordCard.voice: Vismaad, wonder: twenty-four pauris and their saloks, sung at dawn, hold vismaad, awe, truth, sweetness, and the thread of compassion.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: the ballad in Rag Asa, Guru Nanak's var of twenty-four pauris.

carryVoice: Your line: wonder at dawn. One line, carried out the door, is plenty. Four weeks of the dawn ballad, complete.
